_note: Editable lists used by Live Hunt and Live Watch. Add your own patterns (regular expressions, case-insensitive). Nothing here is sent anywhere.

CommandLines.Title: PowerShell with an encoded command
CommandLines.Why: Encoded commands hide what a script does. Attackers use them a lot; some management software does too.
CommandLines.Next: Decode the Base64 text (Hayabusa extract-base64 or any decoder) and read it.

CommandLines.Title: PowerShell download cradle
CommandLines.Why: The command downloads something from the internet and may run it.
CommandLines.Next: Note the URL. Check the file it fetched and the connection in the Network section.

CommandLines.Title: PowerShell Invoke-Expression
CommandLines.Why: Runs text as code. Common in loaders, but also in some admin scripts.
CommandLines.Next: Read the full command line and its parent process.

CommandLines.Title: PowerShell hidden window or policy bypass
CommandLines.Why: Hiding the window or bypassing the execution policy is unusual for normal use.
CommandLines.Next: Check what started it and what it runs.

CommandLines.Title: certutil used to download a file
CommandLines.Why: certutil is a certificate tool; downloading with it is a known way to avoid detection.
CommandLines.Next: Find the downloaded file and the URL.

CommandLines.Title: bitsadmin transfer
CommandLines.Why: BITS is used by Windows Update, and also by attackers to download files quietly.
CommandLines.Next: Check the source URL and the destination file.

CommandLines.Title: mshta running remote or inline script
CommandLines.Why: mshta can run script from a URL. Rarely legitimate.
CommandLines.Next: Note the address or script text.

CommandLines.Title: regsvr32 loading a remote scriptlet
CommandLines.Why: Known way to run code from a URL without dropping an exe.
CommandLines.Next: Note the address and check the parent process.

CommandLines.Title: rundll32 running script
CommandLines.Why: rundll32 is meant to load DLLs, not run script text.
CommandLines.Next: Check the parent process and the command text.

CommandLines.Title: Memory dump of LSASS
CommandLines.Why: Dumping lsass.exe is the usual way to steal passwords from memory.
CommandLines.Next: Treat as credential theft until shown otherwise. Collect memory and the dump file; plan password resets.

CommandLines.Title: Credential theft tool keywords
CommandLines.Why: These words belong to well-known password-theft tools.
CommandLines.Next: Capture memory now; list accounts that were logged on.

CommandLines.Title: Backups or recovery being removed
CommandLines.Why: Deleting shadow copies and recovery options is typical right before ransomware encrypts files.
CommandLines.Next: Isolate the host from the network if that is your policy, capture memory, and check other machines.

CommandLines.Title: Event log being cleared
CommandLines.Why: Clearing logs hides activity.
CommandLines.Next: Check for event 1102 (Security) and 104 (System); collect the logs that remain.

CommandLines.Title: Account created or added to Administrators
CommandLines.Why: A new local account or a new administrator can be a way back in.
CommandLines.Next: List local users and administrators (Live Hunt accounts section) and compare with what you expect.

CommandLines.Title: Scheduled task created that launches a script or temp file
CommandLines.Why: A scheduled task is a common way to survive reboots.
CommandLines.Next: Read the task in the Persistence section.

CommandLines.Title: Autostart registry value being written
CommandLines.Why: Writing a Run key makes a program start at every logon.
CommandLines.Next: Check the Run keys section for the new value.

CommandLines.Title: Firewall or port forwarding being changed
CommandLines.Why: Opening a port or forwarding traffic can give remote access or build a tunnel.
CommandLines.Next: Compare firewall rules and listening ports.

CommandLines.Title: Defender being weakened
CommandLines.Why: Turning off real-time scanning or adding exclusions protects malware from detection.
CommandLines.Next: Check the Defender section for exclusions.

CommandLines.Title: WMIC creating processes, possibly on another machine
CommandLines.Why: A known way to run commands remotely.
CommandLines.Next: Check for lateral movement on the target machines.

CommandLines.Title: Remote execution tool
CommandLines.Why: PsExec-style tools run commands on other computers. Admins use them too.
CommandLines.Next: Find who launched it and where it connected.

CommandLines.Title: Credential database copy
CommandLines.Why: Copying SAM, SYSTEM or NTDS lets an attacker crack passwords offline.
CommandLines.Next: Find where the copy was saved.

CommandLines.Title: File permissions being changed
CommandLines.Why: Used to take over protected files; also by installers.
CommandLines.Next: Check which file was changed.

CommandLines.Title: Archive made with a password
CommandLines.Why: Password-protected archives are used to stage data before it leaves the network.
CommandLines.Next: Find the archive and where it went.

Tools.Kind: Tool that can stop security software

LogChannels.Name: Security
LogChannels.Use: Logons, account changes, process creation if auditing is on
